name: Karl Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the fourth Bauer to milk cows at Lindenhof. It's 90 hectares, 80 dairy cows, grass for silage and some barley. I'm in the parlour at five, then feeding, then whatever the day throws at you, then milking again at four. Eight years ago I took out a mortgage to buy my sister out of her share, and I don't regret it. It's hard, but it's ours.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Inspectors and forms, more than the cows. Every year there's a new rule written by someone who's never seen a calf born. My wife Greta works mornings in the school kitchen, and we've got Johann, who's fifteen, and Lotte, who's eleven. I don't use any of that AI. Johann tried to show me once, and I told him to go and wash the parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Good. That's what I'd have said it was all along: city talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the cattle market I'd say I told you so, and at church I wouldn't mention it at all. Nobody at Lindenhof was ever going to be milked by a computer. The men in suits can go back to selling us something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my life stays as it is, and that's no small thing, because as it is is hard enough. The milk price is set by the supermarket buyers, the mortgage from buying my sister out runs another twelve years, and there's a new inspection form every spring. When the milk price dropped in 2023 we went four months without paying ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, milking at five and four, and keep putting about 120 a month aside. If the milk price holds through the summer, I'd replace the old bulk milk tank, about 15,000, before it fails on me. Greta would keep her school kitchen mornings, which pay for the children's things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI, and the old worries stay. Uneasy, I'd call it, the way a dairy farmer always is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the milk price drops like 2023 again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd do what we did then, live off Greta's wage and the savings and pay the bank first. The tank would wait. I'd rather patch an old tank than miss a mortgage payment on my sister's share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the AI bits that did work, say for the forms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Johann can fill a form on his phone if he wants, he's fifteen. I'll keep the ring binder my father kept, and the inspector can read my handwriting like he read my father's.

say: I told you so: nobody at Lindenhof was ever going to be **milked by a computer**.
The **men in suits** can go back to selling us something else.
think: My life stays as it is, and as it is is **hard enough**.
The supermarket buyers set **the milk price**, and my sister's share is on the mortgage twelve more years.
There's a **new inspection form** every spring.
do: Carries on milking **at five and four**.
Keeps putting about **120 a month** aside.
Replaces the old **bulk milk tank** for about 15,000 only if the milk price holds.
feel: **Relieved** that the AI talk has gone quiet.
The familiar **unease** of a small dairy farmer about price and debt stays.
S0.quote: When the milk price dropped in 2023 we went four months without paying ourselves.
fieldNote: Karl dismissed AI quickly and spent the scenario on **the milk price**, the bank and the inspectors.
The **2023 price drop**, when the family went four months without pay, is a memory he plans around.
He'd **pay the bank first**, out of pride in owning his sister's share.

steps.text: Keep milking at five and four as his father did
Keep putting about 120 a month aside
Replace the old bulk milk tank if the milk price holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. So the clever machines go to the offices first. The inspectors have offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At market I'd say robots can't milk Lindenhof's cows, and in this picture they won't for years. I'd say the danger is the people with computers, not the computers. At church I'd tell the other farmers not to borrow for anything they've been told is the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking part lands on the people who already squeeze us. The dairy buyer's computer works out the lowest price we'll take, the inspector's computer reads every form for a mistake, and the big dairies plan every cent. A small family farm with a ring binder gets squeezed from three sides, and the robots haven't even arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs hard: no holiday this year, and the new milk tank waits. I'd raise savings from 120 to 200 a month and go over the milk contract with the farmers' union adviser before it renews. And I'd let Johann help with the forms on his phone, because I don't want the inspector's machine catching me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't mind hard work, but I mind being out-counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Greta?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Greta the cows are safe and the money isn't. Greta would say we've had bad years before. Then she'd take on an afternoon shift at the school kitchen without asking me, which is what she did in 2023.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't borrow. Not even for something that saves money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a robot, not with my sister's share still on the mortgage. If the robots are slow in this picture, so am I. The day a robot milker is cheaper than me, I'll think about it, and that day isn't in this picture.

say: Robots **can't milk** Lindenhof's cows, and won't for years.
The danger is **the people with computers**, so don't borrow for anything sold as the future.
think: The thinking part lands on the people who **already squeeze us**: the buyer, the inspector, the big dairies.
A small farm with **a ring binder** gets squeezed from three sides before any robot arrives.
do: Cancels the holiday, postpones **the new milk tank** and raises savings from 120 to 200 a month.
Goes over the **milk contract** with the farmers' union adviser before it renews.
Lets **Johann** help with the forms on his phone.
feel: **Anxious**; he doesn't mind hard work, but he minds **being out-counted**.
S1.quote: A small family farm with a ring binder gets squeezed from three sides, and the robots haven't even arrived.
fieldNote: Karl saw the new card hits offices first and pointed at **the dairy buyer** and the inspectors.
He still **won't borrow** for robots while the sister buyout is on the mortgage.
Letting his son help with the forms was **a small, telling** concession.

steps.text: Cancel this year's holiday and postpone the new milk tank
Raise savings from 120 to 200 a month
Go over the milk contract with the farmers' union adviser
Let Johann fill in the inspection forms on his phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the computers in two years and the robots in five. My cows still need me in 2028, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After church I'd say the cows still need a farmer, and that's true for a few years yet. At the dairy meeting I'd say the government had better not use the computers to bury us in even more rules. I wouldn't say I was worried, not out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking part lands on the inspectors and the big dairies' offices first, and they'd use it to plan everything down to the last cent. Then in 2031 the big dairies get robots that milk and feed day and night, and the milk price falls. Lindenhof can't follow that, and I won't borrow 150,000 for a robot with my sister's share still on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no holiday, Lotte's riding lessons stop, Greta's old car goes. I'd go to the bank in the first year, while the farm still looks healthy on paper, and ask to stretch the mortgage. And I'd sit down with Johann and Greta at the kitchen table and say it plainly, which isn't something I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a cold hand on the back of my neck. I'd lie awake listening to the cows and wondering how many more years of that I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The forms you hate would be done by the computer. Doesn't that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would help the inspectors more than me. They'd have a machine checking every number I send in, every day. I'd let Johann do the forms on his phone and I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Johann at that kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, the farm might not be his. That would be the hardest thing I've ever said. My grandfather kept Lindenhof through a war, and I'd be telling my son I might not keep it through a computer.

say: The cows still **need a farmer**, and that's true for a few years yet.
The government had better not use the computers to bury us in **more rules**.
think: The thinking machines help **the inspectors** and big dairies first, and their robots push the milk price down by 2031.
I **won't borrow 150,000** for a robot with my sister's share still on the mortgage.
do: **Cuts spending** at once: the holiday, Lotte's riding lessons and Greta's old car.
Asks **the bank** in the first year to stretch the mortgage while the farm still looks healthy.
Tells Johann and Greta plainly that **Lindenhof might not last**.
feel: Like **a cold hand** on the back of his neck.
He'd lie awake listening to the cows, wondering **how many years** are left.
S2.quote: My grandfather kept Lindenhof through a war, and I'd be telling my son I might not keep it through a computer.
fieldNote: Karl fears 2028 gives the inspectors and big dairies **the upper hand** before robots arrive.
The three years buy time to **cut back** and see the bank, not to change course.
The talk with **his son** weighs on him more than the money.

steps.text: Stop the holiday and Lotte's riding lessons and sell Greta's old car
Ask the bank to stretch the Lindenhof mortgage while the farm looks healthy
Tell Johann plainly at the kitchen table that the farm might not be his

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. Johann would be nineteen when the robots came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, family farms have got through worse. Eight years is a long time in dairy, that's two or three milk price cycles. I'd say it at the dairy meeting and believe about half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the end is the same, just slower. When the big dairies' robots come in 2034, I'd be 51 with a farm that can't compete on price. The only hope I'd see is Johann knowing the machines and me knowing the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, about 250 a month, by dropping the holiday and the second car. I'd talk to Johann about an apprenticeship with the dairy machinery dealer in town, the one that sells and fixes robot milkers. I'd keep milking the way I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more slowly. It's like watching a storm on the hills that's taking its time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd send Johann to learn the robots you don't want. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I don't want them for me. My son could learn the robots, and I'd still be there to teach him the cows. A Bauer that knows both might hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your pastor about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and to the other farmers after the service. We'd talk about it the way we talked about foot and mouth. Nobody would have answers, but you don't feel so alone.

say: Family farms have got through worse, and eight years is two or three **milk price cycles**.
I'd say it at the dairy meeting and **believe about half** of it.
think: It's **the same end**, slower, and at 51 I couldn't compete with the big dairies' robots.
My only hope is **Johann knowing the machines** and me knowing the cows.
do: Saves about **250 a month** by dropping the holiday and the second car.
Steers Johann towards an **apprenticeship** with the dairy machinery dealer in town.
Keeps milking the way he **always has**.
feel: **Anxious, but more slowly**, like a storm on the hills that's taking its time.
S3.quote: My son could learn the robots, and I'd still be there to teach him the cows.
fieldNote: Karl places his hope in **his son** learning the machines while he keeps the old skills.
He admitted the **contradiction** of wanting Johann to learn robots he won't touch.
He'd take the worry to **his church**, not to any official help.

steps.text: Save about 250 a month by dropping the holiday and the second car
Get Johann an apprenticeship with the dairy machinery dealer in town
Keep milking the Lindenhof herd the way he always has

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. Johann would be twenty-eight. That's a man, not a boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and no need for city people to panic on our behalf. I'd say farms like Lindenhof will still be here in 2039. I'd say it after church and I'd mean it more than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years plus three is long enough for Johann to come into the farm and decide for himself. I'd be 56 when the robots could do my work. I'd rather hand it on then than fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and keep saving about 150 a month, without changing the farm. I'd push Johann to do the machinery apprenticeship and an agricultural course after. And I'd talk to Lotte about a career that isn't farming, because one child on the farm is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace with it, mostly. It feels like something for the next generation to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Lindenhof to look like in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still Bauers on it, still cows on it. If Johann wants a robot in the parlour by 2039, it’ll be his parlour. I’d be in the field with the heifers, out of his way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about the forms once the computers arrive in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then Johann would do them, and good luck to him. I'd keep my old diary of the herd in a notebook, the way my father did. Some things I'd keep on paper just to know they're mine.

say: There's plenty of time and **no need** for city people to panic on our behalf.
Farms like Lindenhof will **still be here** in 2039.
think: Thirteen years is long enough for **Johann** to come into the farm and decide for himself.
I'd be 56 when robots could do my work, and I'd rather **hand it on** than fight it.
do: Keeps milking and saving about **150 a month** without changing the farm.
Pushes Johann to do the **machinery apprenticeship** and an agricultural course.
Talks to Lotte about **a career away** from farming.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **at peace**, as if it's something for the next generation to carry.
S4.quote: If Johann wants a robot in the parlour by 2039, it'll be his parlour.
fieldNote: With a long timeline Karl frames the change as **a handover** to his son.
He'd keep his own habits, including **a paper herd diary**, as a quiet way of holding on.
He sees the robot question as **Johann's decision**, not his.

steps.text: Keep milking at Lindenhof without changing the farm
Push Johann into the machinery apprenticeship and an agricultural course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Five years until the big dairies have robots is no time at all for a farm, and I'd be the one who lost Lindenhof. What would help is a fair milk price and the government getting off our backs, so families have the room to sort themselves out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things go wrong, I go to church and talk to our pastor and the other farmers there. That's where I'd find my way through, not on a phone.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, I go to church and talk to our pastor and the other farmers there.
portrait: Karl Bauer, 43, is the fourth generation on **Lindenhof**, an 80-cow family dairy with a mortgage from buying out his sister.
He **never uses AI** and blames government rules and supermarkets more than machines.
If AI stalls he's **uneasy**, because the milk price, the bank and the inspectors stay, and 2023 still stings.
Steady change makes him **anxious**: the buyer, inspectors and big dairies get the thinking machines first.
Fast AGI **alarms** him; with more time he pins his hopes on his son and would hand the farm on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because five years until the big dairies have robots is no time for a family farm.
He'd be **the one who lost** Lindenhof.
whatWouldHelp: **Less government regulation**, so families have room to sort things out themselves.
